steps.say: You just built a pie chart slice. The fraction of people (a quarter) is the same as the fraction of the circle. So angle = fraction × 360°, and turned around, frequency = (angle ÷ 360) × total. That one idea powers every pie chart question.

steps: Bar charts: read a bar's height against the number axis, minding the scale.
Pie charts: frequency = (angle ÷ 360) × total; angle = (frequency ÷ total) × 360.
Scatter graphs: describe correlation and estimate with the line of best fit.
Two-way tables: every row and column adds to its total.
method_card.title: Representing Data
method_card.content:
Pie charts: a sector's angle over 360 is its fraction of the total. Frequency = (angle ÷ 360) × total; angle = (frequency ÷ total) × 360. All sectors add to 360°.

Scatter graphs: positive correlation means both rise together; negative means one rises as the other falls. Read the line of best fit to estimate, but only trust estimates inside the data range.
method_card.example:
A pie chart represents 120 people. The Bus sector is 90°. How many travel by bus?

(90 ÷ 360) × 120 = 30 people

steps: Composite (stacked) bars: read each part, add them for the total, then one part as a percentage: part ÷ total × 100.
Frequency density: for a histogram bar, frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.
Line of best fit: read straight up from the x-value to estimate y; inside the data range (interpolation) is reliable, outside (extrapolation) is not.
gold.title: Gold: composite charts, density and lines of best fit

example.question: A stacked bar shows A = 30, B = 20 in one month. What percentage is A?

steps: Bar charts: follow the top of a bar across to the number axis. Each gridline is worth the scale shown, so a bar 4 gridlines up on a scale of 5 means 20.
Pie sectors: a sector's share is its frequency over the total. Turn a sector into people with (angle ÷ 360) × total.
For 'how many more', read both values, then subtract the smaller from the larger.
bronze.title: Bronze: reading charts and simple pie sectors

example.question: A bar chart shows Green = 15, Blue = 25. How many more chose blue?

steps: Angle to frequency: divide the angle by 360 to get the fraction, then multiply by the total.
Frequency to angle: divide the frequency by the total, then multiply by 360.
Missing angle: all sectors add to 360°, so subtract the known angles from 360.
Two-way tables: each row and column adds to its total, so fill a gap by subtracting.
